item.title: Jack Hughes scores in OT to lift Devils past Red Wings
item.description: Jack Hughes scored on a breakaway 1:19 into overtime to give the New Jersey Devils a 5-4 win over the host Detroit Red Wings on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Jack Hughes scored on a breakaway 1:19 into overtime to give the New Jersey Devils a 5-4 win over the host Detroit Red Wings on Tuesday. Jesper Bratt, who had a goal and an assist in regulation, also assisted on the winner. Evan Rodrigues, Anthony Mantha and Nico Hischier also scored for New Jersey, while Jake Allen made 23 saves. Hughes chipped in two assists. Alex DeBrincat had two goals and an assist for Detroit. Michael Brandsegg-Nygard and Emmitt Finnie each added a goal and an assist, while John Gibson stopped 32 shots. The Devils capitalized on a Wings turnover in their own zone to score first. Stefan Noesen fed the puck to Rodrigues, who scored from the slot, beating Gibson glove side. Mantha was credited with the secondary assist at 6:07 of the first period. Finnie tied it with 1:25 remaining in the period, converting a cross-ice pass from Brandsegg-Nygard and firing a shot from the left circle past Allen's glove. Anton Johansson also collected an assist. A wild second period ended with the Devils leading 4-3. Brandsegg-Nygard briefly gave the Red Wings a lead when he converted a 2-on-1 off a Finnie pass. DeBrincat picked up the second assist. Mantha tied it by scoring near the crease off a setup from Dawson Mercer. With Keegan Kolesar in the penalty box for hooking, New Jersey took a 3-2 lead on Hischier's goal, as he tipped a backhander past Gibson. Bratt and Hughes had the assists. DeBrincat tied it again with a shot near the blue line that deflected off a defender's stick. Axel Sandin-Pellikka and Justin Faulk picked up the assists. Bratt scored the final goal of the period, lifting the puck past a screened Gibson with 3:08 left. Jonas Siegenthaler and Hughes had the assists. DeBrincat tied it at 4-all with 14:14 remaining, one-timing a shot from the left circle off a Moritz Seider pass. Ben Chiarot had the secondary assist. --Field Level Media

item.title: CBA chief Matt Comyn says Australia must retain economic value of AI
item.description: Commonwealth Bank of Australia CEO Matt Comyn said on Wednesday Australia must ensure more of the economic benefits created by AI remain in the country while regulation should work to build trust in the new technology.
item.dc:creator: Scott Murdoch, Roshan Thomas
item.content:encoded: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA.AX) CEO Matt Comyn said on Wednesday Australia must ensure more of the economic benefits created by AI remain in the country while regulation should work to build trust in the new technology. Comyn said CBA, Australia's largest lender, is rolling out AI technologies across its banking portfolio, especially in business banking. The bank has also launched an AI chat within its banking app to selected customers that can access personal and business banking details. Comyn said AI could be the "most significant technology shift we have seen" but warned an official framework was needed as the technology rolls out at a fast pace around the world. "Realising the AI opportunity will require regulation to keep pace," he said at the bank's annual investor meeting in Sydney. "Effective regulation should help build trust in AI while ensuring global technology companies operate in accordance with Australian laws and standards, and that more of the economic value created by AI is captured in Australia." Australia has started to toughen its approach to AI regulation after initially giving an unconditional welcome to AI companies. The Labor government has responded to community pushback against AI and data centre development by saying it would take a tougher approach. The government has said it is [USN:L4N45G0G8 TEXT:"preparing"] a wide-ranging set of AI laws to take effect from early 2027, which would include limits to water and energy use by data centres, as well as copyright protections and cybersecurity measures. Comyn said Australia's economy remained resilient, although more frequent and volatile international shocks were likely. "It will take time for higher interest rates to bring inflation back into the target range," Comyn said. The remarks come a day after minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia's [USN:P8N44M01S TEXT:"September meeting"] showed the board remained concerned about persistent inflation pressures and considered further rate hikes could be needed if price growth proved more stubborn than expected. The central bank last month [USN:L4N45L00R TEXT:"ordered"] a fourth interest rate rise for the year which took the official cash rate to 4.6%, the highest level in 15 years. Comyn said Australia had little control over external shocks and would need to boost productivity through measures including building more homes, delivering reliable low-cost energy at scale and adopting technologies such as AI across the economy. In his address to shareholders, CBA Chair Paul O'Malley said cost-of-living pressures and higher interest rates continued to affect households unevenly, while businesses were managing elevated input costs and supply uncertainty. [USN:L2N3VW00W TEXT:"Succession planning remained a focus"] for the lender, O'Malley said, a year after telling shareholders Comyn would remain in the CEO role for at least another three years.

item.title: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say
item.description: The strategy includes a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Parisa Hafezi, Jonathan Saul, Phil Stewart
item.content:encoded: Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters. Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war , in an effort to gain leverage over Washington. Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up [USN:L1N45Z00X TEXT:"oil prices"], though some oil has [USN:L6N42O131 TEXT:"continued to transit"]. The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said. "The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said. The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said. IRAN USING SPOTTERS A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said. Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy. The war — and its [USN:L6N4530XO TEXT:"$3 billion monthly price tag"] — has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November's midterm elections , which will decide control of Congress. US President Donald Trump has been [USN:L1N45T10U TEXT:"weighing next steps"] against Iran, but has said he [USN:L1N45U0PH TEXT:"will not attack"] again before the vote. The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and [USN:L1N45U0QQ TEXT:"extending sanctions"] as it tries to pile [USN:L6N45K0UX TEXT:"economic pressure"] on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict. The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic. In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have [USN:L1N45T0HL TEXT:"surged to their highest level"] since the war began, according to independent data. There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on October 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization. "There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said. ATTACKS OVER AN EXPANDED AREA As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said. Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days. The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections. "Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said. "Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz." The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. COMPLETE CLOSURE OF HORMUZ SOON, SAYS IRANIAN OFFICIAL Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said. In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe", the second-highest level. "IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said.

item.title: Ukrainian ex-officer stands trial in Germany over Nord Stream bombing
item.description: A Ukrainian ex-military officer goes on trial in Germany on Wednesday, accused of organising the secret operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in September 2022, severing western Europe from the biggest source of Russian natural gas.
item.dc:creator: Miranda Murray
item.content:encoded: A Ukrainian ex-military officer goes on trial in Germany on Wednesday, accused of organising the secret operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in September 2022, severing western Europe from the biggest source of Russian natural gas. The suspect, identified under German privacy rules only as Serhii K., is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert to mount one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times. The case will provide the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the crime. Prosecutors have alleged that Serhii K., who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with other members of the military to plan the [USN:L8N3UD0YM TEXT:"clandestine operation"] on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities. Serhii K. has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-km (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline. The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. The Russian government said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation. German prosecutors say the actions Serhii K. is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime. The alleged aim was to disrupt a major source of foreign revenue for Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched earlier that year. He is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have [USN:L6N44H0T9 TEXT:"arrested"] another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the [USN:SPN44900E TEXT:"divers in the team"]. The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Germany previously received half its natural gas imports through the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, by far the biggest and most modern Russian pipeline serving western Europe, which allowed Russia to bypass Soviet-era pipelines transiting Ukraine. The supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built although Berlin cancelled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. PLUMES OF METHANE GASE The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could also have domestic political implications. Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow. In the initial months after the pipelines were attacked, Western officials mainly pointed fingers at Russia. Moscow has always denied any involvement and called the suggestion it would blow up its own pipelines absurd. It also rejects charges that it has more recently targeted Western infrastructure with so-called "hybrid" sabotage and drone attacks. The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 metres under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic metres of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries. On September 26, 2022, several blasts, some 17 hours apart, were detected by Swedish seismologists. The blasts sent huge plumes of methane gas into the atmosphere as three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines were ruptured. Prosecutors allege that Serhii K. travelled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. They say he and his group used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialised military-grade explosives fitted with timers to the sea floor. The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on September 6 and returned on September 23, 2022.

item.title: BHP's Escondida, supervisors hold talks in bid to avert strike
item.description: In a last-ditch effort to avoid a strike, the supervisors' union at BHP's Escondida copper mine in Chile and company representatives are holding talks, the union said late on Tuesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: In a last-ditch effort to avoid a strike, the supervisors' union at BHP's (BHP.AX) Escondida copper mine in Chile and company representatives are holding talks, the union said late on Tuesday. Earlier in the day, the union announced it would begin a strike on Wednesday after mediation efforts to tie up a new collective labor contract had failed. The union was summoned to government-mediated talks to hold another meeting with the company and will be giving updates on the negotiations, the union said in a message sent to its members seen by Reuters The possibility of a strike at the world's largest copper mine has been supporting copper prices as any stoppage would tighten global supply A BHP spokesperson in Chile did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The supervisors' union has been embroiled in fraught contract negotiations with Escondida for several weeks, and has been threatening a strike if talks were to fail Earlier on Tuesday, the union said it made an offer incorporating 90% of company proposals plus key union demands including salary increases and production bonuses The union said the company demanded workers give up essential benefits and insisted on sharing private biometric data with third parties Escondida, in Chile's northern Atacama Desert, is majority-owned and operated by BHP. Rio Tinto (RIO.L) (RIO.AX) holds a 30% stake and Japan-based JECO owns 12.5%.

item.title: Supervisores de mina chilena Escondida y empresa retoman diálogo en último intento por evitar huelga
item.description: Los supervisores de la chilena Escondida, el mayor yacimiento mundial de cobre y controlado por BHP, retomaron sorpresivamente el diálogo con la empresa a última hora del martes en un último intento por evitar una huelga, luego de que habían anunciado que iniciarían la paralización el miércoles.
item.dc:creator: Fabián Andrés Cambero
item.content:encoded: Los supervisores de la chilena Escondida, el mayor yacimiento mundial de cobre y controlado por BHP, retomaron sorpresivamente el diálogo con la empresa a última hora del martes en un último intento por evitar una huelga, luego de que habían anunciado que iniciarían la paralización el miércoles. El riesgo de una paralización en la mina ha estado apoyando los precios globales del metal en medio de los temores por una escasez de oferta. El sindicato había dicho inicialmente en un comunicado que no recibió respuesta a una propuesta que había formulado en la víspera y anunció que la huelga "se hará efectiva mañana 14 de octubre a contar del primer turno de trabajo". Sin embargo, horas más tarde el gremio envió un mensaje a sus socios donde informó que fueron "citados por la dirección del trabajo para tener nuevamente una reunión con la empresa. Estaremos comunicando cualquier novedad". La última propuesta presentada por la empresa mantenía pagos finales y préstamo blando por unos 30.000 dólares por socio. La empresa no respondió inmediatamente a una solicitud de comentarios. Sin embargo, en un boletín interno, Escondida confirmó que se iniciaría la paralización a las 8.00 local (1100 GMT) del miércoles pero acotó que la oferta mantenía su vigencia hasta la medianoche del martes y que la dirigencia sindical tenía "la facultad legal de aceptar la oferta hasta esa hora". En la tarde, el sindicato 1 de trabajadores emitió un boletín interno a sus socios donde los instó a suspender y abandonar sus labores en caso de que, a falta de supervisión, pudiera haber un riesgo inminente para su salud o vida.

item.title: Galderma agrees to buy ZO Skin Health for around $1.5 billion, sources say
item.description: Swiss skincare conglomerate Galderma has agreed to buy medical-grade skincare company ZO Skin Health for around $1.5 billion, according to two people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Abigail Summerville
item.content:encoded: Swiss skincare conglomerate Galderma (GALD.S) has agreed to buy medical-grade skincare company ZO Skin Health for around $1.5 billion, according to two people familiar with the matter. A deal could be announced in the coming days, the people said. ZO and Galderma, which were contacted outside regular business hours, did not immediately respond to requests for comment. ZO's owner, investment firm Blackstone (BX.N) , was exploring a sale of the company with investment banks Citigroup (C.N) and Raymond James (RJF.N) , Reuters [USN:L6N4500XQ TEXT:"reported"] last month. Blackstone declined to comment on Tuesday. The move by dermatology company Galderma, in which beauty giant L'Oréal (OREP.PA) owns a 20% stake, will expand its presence in the US market. In August, the company opened a US and Latin America headquarters in Miami. Established in 1981, Galderma also owns skincare brands Cetaphil and Alastin Skincare, Differin Epiduo acne gel, injectable neurotoxin Dysport, and dermal filler brand Restylane. Many strategic buyers are prioritizing clinically backed, physician-distributed skincare brands like ZO because of their efficacy and steadier demand versus over-the-counter products. Dermatologist Zein Obagi founded ZO in 2007. ZO sells skincare products including cleansers, serums, exfoliators and toners that are distributed by physicians and skincare professionals. Blackstone acquired ZO through its tactical opportunities fund in 2020.

item.title: Zelenskiy visits Britain as Burnham pledges fresh support for Ukraine
item.description: Britain has said it does not support the US-Russia diesel deal, and called for allies to keep up the economic pressure on Moscow.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy will meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London on Wednesday as Britain looks to reaffirm its support for Ukraine, including with the promise of a new package of surface-to-air missiles. The meeting comes at a difficult time for Zelenskiy. US President Donald Trump said at the weekend he [USN:L6N45W06G TEXT:"should be replaced"] as Ukraine's leader, days after cutting a deal with Moscow to [USN:L4N45Y0AR TEXT:"lift sanctions"] on Russian diesel exports. Britain has said it does not support the US-Russia diesel deal, and called for allies to keep up the economic pressure on Moscow. "My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer, we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe," Burnham said in a statement before the meeting. Burnham said backing for Ukraine was vital to keeping people in Britain safe and pledged further military support. He announced the planned delivery of £45 million ($59.60 million) of surface-to-air missiles used to target jet-powered Russian drones, with £10 million of that package fast-tracked to meet an urgent need in Ukraine. Burnham has asked officials to draw up further sanctions, military aid, and fiscal support, and his foreign and finance ministers have been lobbying allies to follow Britain in banning maritime services that support Russian liquefied natural gas exports. ($1 = 0.7551 pounds)

item.title: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion by US government for failing to police suspicious activity
item.description: Bank of America has been fined $1.21 billion by US regulators for widespread failures to detect potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings.
item.dc:creator: Pete Schroeder, Ismail Shakil, Saeed Azhar
item.content:encoded: Bank of America (BAC.N) has been fined $1.21 billion by US regulators for widespread failures to detect potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings. The Treasury Department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank's failure to report more than $5 billion in suspicious activity to the government, including $1 billion that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks. "Financial institutions are on the front lines of protecting our economic and national security," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks." The Treasury said the bank "prioritized its revenues" in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. The consent order requires Bank of America to hire an independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that the bank failed to detect at the time, and report those transactions to FinCEN. "Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right," said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. "We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators." The spokesperson added that the bank's third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion, which will reduce quarterly net income by approximately 17 cents a share. Analysts have estimated adjusted EPS of $1.10, according to mean estimates compiled by LSEG, but that excludes one-offs like this fine. Shares were down 2.7% in after-hours trading after closing the day down 1.1%. The penalty is likely to add to negative investor sentiment and raise concerns about higher expenses and whether Bank of America can maintain its roughly $6 billion quarterly share buyback pace, UBS analyst Erika Najarian said in a note. With earnings due on Wednesday, "we think shares likely underperforming at open," she said. She noted there was no asset cap, a regulatory penalty that would limit how large the bank could grow. REGULATOR SAYS COMPLIANCE PROGRAM 'DEFICIENT AND INEFFECTIVE' As part of the fine, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency levied a $750 million civil penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money laundering programs that were identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog. The regulator said the bank's compliance program was "deficient and ineffective," and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions. In addition, the bank paid an $11.6 million fine to the Office of Foreign Assets Control for over 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The Treasury said the bank mistakenly processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran. The fine comes days after American Express [USN:L6N45U1AT TEXT:"was also hit with a $350 million penalty"] for similar anti-money laundering shortcomings.

item.title: Televisa, Fintech to take on America Movil with $2 billion purchase of AT&T's Mexican unit
item.description: Grupo Televisa , and Fintech Holdings have agreed to buy AT&T's Mexican unit for $2 billion in cash, setting up a showdown with telecoms giant America Movil and marking one of Mexico's biggest M&A deals in recent years.
item.dc:creator: Iñigo Alexander
item.content:encoded: Grupo Televisa (TLEVISACPO.MX) , and Fintech Holdings have agreed to buy AT&T's (T.N) Mexican unit for $2 billion in cash, setting up a showdown with telecoms giant America Movil (AMXB.MX) and marking one of Mexico's biggest M&A deals in recent years. News of the deal, described as a "bargain" by Scotiabank, sent shares in Televisa, Mexico's largest broadcaster and the world's largest producer of Spanish-language content, surging 5% in after-hours trading on the New York Stock Exchange. AT&T's Mexican unit, the country's second-largest mobile operator after America Movil's Telcel, had some 24.7 million subscribers as of December, Televisa said. The deal will give Televisa considerable scale, lifting its share of total fixed and wireless subscribers in Mexico to 19% from 8%, according to the Scotiabank note to clients. "We think the low price tag and Fintech involvement is, in itself, bad news for (America Movil), as it means the new owners can focus more resources in capex," Scotiabank said. Fintech, a private investment firm and holding company owned by the Mexican billionaire David Martinez, owns 22.3% of Televisa and will take a 50% stake in the purchasing consortium. It is Televisa's second attempt to enter the competitive telecommunications sector, after an unsuccessful effort between 2012 and 2014. Despite Mexico's large population, its proximity to the US, and growing demand for connectivity, establishing a foothold in the sector has long proven a challenge due to high costs and fierce competition from Telcel. Scotiabank said the new venture could seek a direct-to-cell partnership with operators like Starlink to compete with Telcel, which operates twice as many connectivity towers and runs a much stronger 5G network throughout the country. For AT&T, the sale will allow it to concentrate on its US fiber and 5G businesses, as it pours more resources into "advanced connectivity" for an AI-enabled future. Shares in AT&T gained 1.6% to close at $22.85. The deal is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027, pending regulatory approvals in Mexico. The price is subject to adjustments, plus additional contractual and contingent benefits, and will be funded through available cash and non-recourse secured debt financing, Televisa said. AT&T is not the only company to depart the Mexican telecoms sector. Spanish telecoms giant Telefonica Movistar in April [USN:L6N40R03P TEXT:"sold its Mexico business"] to a US-led consortium for $450 million as it shifts its focus onto core markets in Europe. AT&T's Mexican unit ended 2025 with revenue of 85.4 billion pesos ($4.65 billion) and operating income of 1.4 billion pesos, Televisa said. ($1 = 18.36 Mexican pesos)

item.title: Cornell bans fraternity parties for rest of academic year after alleged gang rape
item.description: The measure is the strongest reaction yet from Cornell's leadership to a lawsuit filed by a former undergraduate alleging seven men sexually assaulted her during a party.
item.dc:creator: Maria Tsvetkova
item.content:encoded: Cornell University will ban parties and social events at fraternity houses until the end of the academic year, its president said on Tuesday, responding to the outcry over an alleged gang rape on campus in 2024. The measure is the strongest reaction yet from Cornell's leadership to a lawsuit [USN:L1N45T0PE TEXT:"filed by a former undergraduate"], Jane Doe, alleging seven men sexually assaulted her during a party. Over the last several weeks, the Ivy League school in Ithaca, New York, and its president, Michael Kotlikoff, have come under heavy criticism from students, faculty and donors over its response to the allegations. The suspension of parties and social events will apply to Interfraternity Council houses. The council website says Cornell currently has 34 fraternity houses. "These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue," Kotlikoff said in the statement. The Cornell Interfraternity Council did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Prosecutors reopened the investigation into the alleged gang rape after the lawsuit was filed. New York state Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as an independent special prosecutor in the case, citing the earlier failure to protect the alleged victim. President Donald Trump repeated on Tuesday his call to take James, his longtime critic and an elected Democrat, off the case. "The Governor should take James off this case, immediately," Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump first questioned James' appointment in early October, but his comments did not prompt any action by officials. The offices of Hochul and the attorney general did not immediately reply to requests for comment. Since the [USN:L1N45K0ML TEXT:"lawsuit"] against seven fraternity members, the university and others was filed in September, the Cornell administration has faced student protests, a pending no-confidence resolution from faculty, criticism by alumni and a public assembly where students blamed university officials for tolerating what they described as a culture of sexual violence. None of the men named in the lawsuit have been criminally charged. "I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell," Kotlikoff said. "Women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe," he said, adding that additional staff would be hired to support survivors of sexual assault. Cornell will also work with New York State Police to investigate incidents, he said, and accelerate previous recommendations put forward by a task force on sexual violence. Thirty-five percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing non-consensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since entering Cornell, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website. "We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," Kotlikoff said.

item.title: Glencore shares trade higher on ASX debut as investors eye copper
item.description: Glencore's , shares started trading on the Australian Securities Exchange on Wednesday at a small premium to their London close, as the miner and trader hopes to secure a better valuation from investors seeking greater copper exposure.
item.dc:creator: Melanie Burton
item.content:encoded: Glencore's (GLEN.L) , shares started trading on the Australian Securities Exchange on Wednesday at a small premium to their London close, as the miner and trader hopes to secure a better valuation from investors seeking greater copper exposure. Glencore CEO Gary Nagle expects strong demand from Australian investors betting on copper's role in [USN:L8N45U2BV TEXT:"electrification"], he said on Friday, as demand rises for the metal's use in power grid expansions, transport and AI data centres. “Glencore has been investing in Australia for decades and we know the Australian investment community has a sophisticated understanding of global resources and commodity markets,” Nagle said in a statement on Wednesday. Glencore CHESS Depositary Interests (CDIs) opened at A$11.44 ($7.99), or 603 pence. On Tuesday, Glencore closed at 582.90 pence on the London Stock Exchange. The Switzerland-based company's CDIs are trading in a market home to other large miners like BHP Group (BHP.AX) , Rio Tinto (RIO.AX) , (RIO.L) and Fortescue <FMG.AX>, whose shares all edged down in early trading. Glencore shares already trade in London with another secondary listing in Johannesburg. Nagle has previously said he believes the $88 billion company can achieve inclusion in Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index (.AXJO) within 12 months, but analysts see momentum behind the stock potentially propelling it into the top indexes in [USN:L4N3Z11V1 TEXT:"half that time"]. "It is not every day that a company of Glencore’s scale joins the ASX, particularly in a period of subdued listing activity," said Paul Schroder, a partner at law firm Mallesons. "Its arrival is a significant addition to the Australian market and reinforces the ASX’s standing as a leading resources exchange." BUYOUT OPPORTUNITIES Analysts and investors speculated Glencore's decision to list Down Under could help acclimatise those [USN:L8N44B03D TEXT:"who had not seen value"] in its approach to Rio Tinto last year. Rio Tinto walked away from takeover talks with Glencore in February, ending months of negotiations over a $240 billion tie-up that would have reshaped the global mining industry. Nagle told reporters last week that a deeper local presence in Australia, where it produces coal, copper, zinc, lead and nickel, may [USN:L8N45U2BV TEXT:"yield business opportunities"], although it had no set buyout list. JPMorgan analysts said on Friday after a meeting with Nagle that Glencore's management team still saw merits in a combination with Rio Tinto and noted its shares had outperformed its Anglo-Australian rival by 10% since negotiations collapsed in February. "M&A is seen as part of the growth strategy and it was noted 'who knows what happens in the future,'" the analysts said in a report. ($1 = 0.7546 pounds, 1.4320 Australian dollars) (1 British pound = 1.8988 Australian dollars)

item.title: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI engineer over covert recording device, DOJ says
item.description: The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research.
item.dc:creator: Jaspreet Singh
item.content:encoded: US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was. OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department. The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins. The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings. "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said. OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi embassy in the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. "Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement. Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through September 16, according to the FBI complaint. He has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020. If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine and three years of supervised release. A LinkedIn profile showed that Alfozan studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said. Reuters could not independently verify the details mentioned in his LinkedIn profile. Separately, the Information reported that OpenAI was in early talks to acquire Trail of Bits, a startup that identifies and fixes vulnerabilities in open-source software. The talks were ongoing and could fall apart, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter. OpenAI and Trail of Bits did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. OpenAI said on Friday it fired three researchers after an investigation found they had violated company policies on handling sensitive information. The researchers, Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, had published a letter detailing the circumstances of their dismissal and arguing that the abrupt firings could create uncertainty among employees and undermine a culture in which researchers could raise safety concerns.
