item.title: 'Gift to our adversary': More Republicans criticize Trump's Russia diesel deal
item.description: The lawmakers' letter to Trump said the agreement provides Russian President Putin's government with more fuel to finance its war, and will not benefit Americans.
item.dc:creator: Patricia Zengerle, Valerie Volcovici
item.content:encoded: A dozen US senators, including six Republicans, called on President Donald Trump on Tuesday to rescind his diesel deal with Russia , days before his administration must decide whether to formally impose new sanctions on Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The lawmakers' letter to Trump said the agreement provides Russian President Vladimir Putin's government with more fuel to finance its war , and will not benefit Americans, adding to a torrent of congressional criticism since Trump announced the deal on Friday. The resistance marks a shift from what had been Republicans' near-unanimous support for Trump's foreign policy decisions, weeks before November 3 midterm elections that will determine whether the party retains control of Congress. In his post, Trump said he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports, and that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. Although Trump said he wanted to reduce prices, the amount he referenced is less than a day's supply for the US transport sector alone, according to US Energy Information Administration data, which shows daily use of around 2.94 million barrels per day. "Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war," the lawmakers said in their letter. "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," they said. The senators' letter, dated Tuesday, was signed by Republicans Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Susan Collins of Maine, Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and John Cornyn of Texas, as well as six Democrats. GRAHAM SANCTIONS BILL DEADLINE LOOMS Under [USN:L1N4570ZO TEXT:"a law"] Trump signed last month, he faces an October 18 deadline to impose sweeping new sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy over the Ukraine war, or waive them because he has determined that doing so is in the national interest. The letter urged Trump to execute the sanctions authorities included in the new law, called the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026", in honor of the late senator, a Russia hawk and close Trump ally who died in July. The administration has not yet told lawmakers whether it would impose the sanctions or issue a waiver. Collins, Murkowski and Tillis had joined Democrats in a [USN:O8N43T024 TEXT:"joint statement"] on Sunday calling on Trump to "reverse course" on [USN:S0N43U024 TEXT:"the deal"], saying it runs counter to US law barring imports of energy until Russia ends its aggression against Ukraine. Earlier on Tuesday, the Republican president [USN:S0N435010 TEXT:"was asked"] whether anyone had told him Russia could use proceeds of the diesel deal to purchase more bombs. "No, nobody told me anything," Trump responded, adding the deal benefited not just the US but the world. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak [USN:S8N45E0D7 TEXT:"said on Monday"] that Russia will be able to return diesel exports to levels above those Trump had outlined under the deal. The Democratic senators who signed the letter were Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Durbin of Illinois, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Jack Reed of Rhode Island and Chris Coons of Connecticut.

item.title: Saudi Arabia plans hybrid format for marquee FII conference after attacks, sources say
item.description: Saudi Arabia plans to make its flagship investment conference a hybrid event, giving executives the option to tune in remotely, after deadly weekend attacks on Riyadh airport prompted a rethink of travel to the kingdom, said two people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari
item.content:encoded: Saudi Arabia plans to make its flagship investment conference a hybrid event, giving executives the option to tune in remotely, after deadly [USN:L6N45Y0C1 TEXT:"weekend attacks on Riyadh airport"] prompted a rethink of travel to the kingdom, said two people familiar with the matter. Some participants were still expected to fly in and could land at airstrips outside Riyadh, or even in neighbouring Gulf states, and then drive to the capital to attend the Future Investment Initiative scheduled for later this month, said one of the people. The Saudi government media office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Earlier this month organisers [USN:L8N45W01K TEXT:"said the event would go ahead"] despite missile attacks in the kingdom. Asked for comment, an FII media representative pointed Reuters to a statement from the CEO and chairman of the FII Institute sent before Saturday's attacks. "As we prepare to welcome thousands of delegates to Riyadh for the exceptional 10th edition of the Future Investment Initiative, their safety and well-being remain our highest priority," said CEO Maha Al Saud and Richard Attias, chairman of the executive committee. 'DAVOS IN THE DESERT' Major oil bosses [USN:L6N45Y0GT TEXT:"dropped out of an international conference"] on Monday and a hybrid model would allow for more participants to take part. The move shows how Saudi Arabia is trying to maintain its push to attract global investment despite an [USN:L1N45Z0HH TEXT:"escalating war with the Houthis"] that has challenged its efforts to turn Riyadh into a hub for global events. The kingdom has used the FII to showcase its plans to diversify its economy from oil and attract foreign investments. The typical attendance of a large number of world leaders, corporate chieftains and financiers has led the event to be nicknamed "Davos in the desert," in a nod to the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Switzerland. Global financial titans, including Goldman Sachs (GS.N) CEO and Chairman David Solomon, Standard Chartered (STAN.L) CEO Bill Winters and Citi's CEO Jane Fraser, were scheduled to participate as speakers at the event, according to a draft programme on the FII website dated October 6. Citi (C.N) and Goldman Sachs declined to comment on the executives' attendance, while Standard Chartered had no immediate comment. The FII event, in its 10th edition, is due to be held at the King Abdulaziz International Conference Centre, on the western edge of Riyadh.

item.title: Russia detains Japanese journalist on suspicion of spying
item.description: Russia's FSB security agency said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist for alleged espionage, and Moscow's Foreign Ministry said it regretted that Tokyo was using correspondents to carry out spying.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia's FSB security agency said on Tuesday it had detained a Japanese journalist for alleged espionage, and Moscow's Foreign Ministry said it regretted that Tokyo was using correspondents to carry out spying. In a statement on its website, the FSB said the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper journalist was detained in the far eastern Sakhalin region on the day before he planned to leave Russia. It did not specify when this was. Russia and Japan, which never signed a formal World War Two peace treaty, have seen their diplomatic relations deteriorate since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, though Japan relies on Russia for supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG). In a statement, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova identified the journalist as Imai Yuki, according to the Russian transliteration of his name, and said his detention cast a new pall on relations with Tokyo. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said on Wednesday that Japan's embassy in Moscow and consulate-general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk had asked Russian authorities for information and called for fair treatment and humanitarian consideration for the Japanese national. Motegi did not confirm the identity of the person detained. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it was still confirming the details. "We will respond with the reporter's safety as our top priority," a spokesperson for the publisher said, declining to comment further. In a Russian state TV video report on the case, three masked men in black uniforms handcuffed a man lying on the ground as a voice off camera said he was suspected of spying. The video showed the man being accompanied by two FSB servicemen onto a plane, then in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for nearly two months. The agency "thwarted the illegal activity" of the journalist, the FSB said. "As a result of intelligence operations, it was established that he gathered and stored information related to the country's defence capabilities in order to pass it on for national intelligence purposes to be used against the security of the Russian Federation," the statement said. "Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia with the status of foreign journalists to gather information for undermining our state's security are regrettable," the foreign ministry spokeswoman said. Japan, she said, had adopted an anti-Russian position during Russia's military campaign in Ukraine and refused to consider Moscow's concerns about Tokyo's "remilitarisation". "We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations," Zakharova said. LONG-RUNNING DISPUTES Russia regards Japan as an [USN:L8N3ZG0NU TEXT:""unfriendly" country"] because it joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine. Russia and Japan have a territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Russian President Vladimir Putin [USN:L8N44F0CG TEXT:"visited"] one of the disputed islands in August, causing uproar in Japan. A delegation from China's Heilongjiang province also visited the island on Tuesday, amid strained relations between Beijing and Tokyo. Japan has said it would continue implementing sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine. This month, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's Cabinet approved additional sanctions against Russia, including expanded export bans and asset freezes targeting individuals affiliated with the Russian military. Asked whether improving US-Russia relations and Japan's reliance on energy imports from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to take countermeasures, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said: "It is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia. "From Japan's perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position. At the same time, Russia is a neighbouring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues." One of the most prominent cases of a foreign journalist arrested in Russia was the detention of [USN:L8N45H0MA TEXT:"Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich"] in 2023. He was found guilty of espionage by a Russian court, sentenced to 16 years and then freed in an East-West prisoner swap in August 2024.

item.title: Hyundai Motor Group bets $15.5 billion on India as global auto hub
item.description: Hyundai Motor Group said on Tuesday it would invest $15.5 billion in India through 2032, deepening its bet on the world's third-largest car market as a key driver of future growth.
item.dc:creator: Surbhi Misra, Nishit Navin
item.content:encoded: Hyundai Motor Group (005380.KS) said on Tuesday it would invest $15.5 billion in India through 2032, deepening its bet on the world's third-largest car market as a key driver of future growth. The South Korean automaker's seven-year plan includes about $700 million of investment in its Indian research and development centre, expansion of production capacity and a dedicated investment entity. India, the world's third-largest car market, is attracting billions of dollars in investment from global automakers seeking to tap rising demand and expand local manufacturing capacity, underscoring its position as a major automotive production hub. Hyundai said last year it would [USN:L3N3VW05E TEXT:"invest "]$5 billion to expand its manufacturing and research operations in India. Japan's Suzuki Motor (7269.T) , the majority owner of India's largest carmaker by volume, Maruti Suzuki, also laid out [USN:L4N3UI0G4 TEXT:"plans "]in 2025 to invest about $8 billion in the country. Carmakers such as Toyota and Honda have [USN:L4N3WC02H TEXT:"committed "]to expanding their manufacturing ambitions in India as well. Hyundai Motor, which employs more than 24,000 people in India, said the investment would create additional jobs across manufacturing, research, engineering and supply chains, but did not disclose a number. The firm said the investment plan, covering 2026 to 2032, would expand manufacturing capacity at Hyundai Motor India and Kia India to support significant volume growth. The investment also includes a vehicle testing track, as part of efforts to develop next-generation automotive technologies. The investment announcement followed a meeting between Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on Tuesday. The group currently has an annual production capacity of more than 1.4 million vehicles in India, comprising 824,000 units at Hyundai's Chennai facilities, 170,000 units at its Pune plant and 431,000 units at Kia's Anantapur facility.

item.title: Wall Street banks see deals slow on market jitters but pipeline is strong
item.description: Wall Street's investment banking and trading stalwarts posted uneven third quarter earnings as both equity and bond markets were rocked by the ongoing Iran war, rising inflation and jitters about the massive spending in the AI buildout.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Wall Street's investment banking and trading stalwarts posted uneven third quarter earnings as both equity and bond markets were rocked by the ongoing Iran war, rising inflation and jitters about the massive spending in the AI buildout. The results from JPMorgan (JPM.N) , Citigroup (C.N) , Goldman Sachs (GS.N) and Wells Fargo (WFC.N) suggest a dealmaking and trading boom [USN:L6N43F12X TEXT:"that powered record first-half earnings"] may be slowing as a grinding bond market rout and equities volatility weighed on activity, particularly in late September, executives said. Still, dealmaking for the third quarter was solid overall with a strong pipeline, while consumers, commercial borrowers and the broader economy remain in good shape, executives said. "The economy continues to be very, very resilient despite some of the headwinds," Goldman CEO David Solomon said on an analyst call. "We have an extraordinary tech supercycle. I think we have a regulatory environment that is really encouraging strategic activity ... I think it's a pretty good environment." A prolonged bond market selloff, which has driven yields around the world to multi-decade highs and put further pressure on stock market valuations, has interrupted dealmaking. [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"The IPO market"] has lost steam in recent weeks, threatening what could have been a banner year for that business. JPMorgan in particular said market volatility and the uncertain economic outlook dampened dealmaking and reduced [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"bond-market trading in recent months"], although its chief financial officer Jeremy Barnum told reporters the deals pipeline remained "very strong." During market turmoil, the gap between buyers and sellers can widen temporarily, but for the most part deals had been delayed rather than canceled, he continued. Analysts have likewise said the IPO market has [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"been selective, not shut"], and delayed offerings could still launch if conditions stabilize during the fourth quarter, a sentiment Solomon echoed. "You might choose to wait, but the IPO market is still in pretty good shape," Solomon said. Citigroup CFO Gonzalo Luchetti [USN:FWN45Z0QV TEXT:"said the bank saw softer investment banking activity"] in the third quarter, while Wells Fargo CFO Mike Santomassimo also pointed to a September slowdown, noting on a call with reporters that the big jump in the benchmark 10-year yield has had an effect. "There is no doubt that high interest rates and the threat of continued Fed hikes is weighing on trading and IB activity in a measurably negative vector," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management. Despite rising prices and borrowing costs, consumers and corporate borrowers remain resilient, with little deterioration in credit quality, JPMorgan and Wells Fargo executives said. "We're just not seeing anything that would imply that there's stress," said Santomassimo. EQUITY STRENGTH PERSISTS Banks also experienced strong trading in equities, as clients rejigged their portfolios on the back of rates uncertainty and surging energy prices. JPMorgan said revenue at its markets division climbed 15% in the third quarter from the prior year, with [USN:L4N45Z10B TEXT:"equity markets revenue surging 49%"]. Goldman beat third-quarter profit estimates, as volatile markets tied to the Middle East conflict[USN:L4N45Z111 TEXT:" lifted its equities revenue"], even as its fixed income, currency and commodities business revenue dropped [USN:L4N45Z111 TEXT:"1% from the year-earlier period"]. Shares were mixed after results, with Wells Fargo and Citigroup lower while JPMorgan and Goldman rose. "Our main concern with this and with other bulge bracket firms remains how much of the 'beats' seem concentrated in the equities trading business and how sustainable they will prove," said Chris Kotowski, analyst at Oppenheimer & Co, in a note.

item.title: Trump fires ambassador to Greece Guilfoyle after reports of misconduct
item.description: The White House said on Tuesday it had asked US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign after a series of news reports raised concerns she sold access to Trump administration officials in exchange for money, gifts and favors.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Bogage , Edward Mcallister, Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: The White House said on Tuesday it had asked US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign after a series of news reports raised concerns she sold access to Trump administration officials in exchange for money, gifts and favors. US President Donald Trump had said on Monday that he was considering firing Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to his son Donald Trump Jr. On Tuesday, he told reporters: "She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading." US lawmakers had raised the alarm after a series of stories in the Wall Street Journal beginning last month that detailed Guilfoyle's conduct, including claims she threatened to use US influence to undermine the Greek government. New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed Guilfoyle had been asked to resign, telling a briefing: "She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well." In a post on X, Guilfoyle repeated denials of wrongdoing and said her gratitude and respect for Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio remained "unwavering." "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote. "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity." One of the reports published by the Journal described Guilfoyle's close relationship with a lobbyist for a Greek energy company and her promotion of that firm, while another cited audio recordings of Guilfoyle bragging about her ties to wealthy Greek businessmen as she sought an invitation to a Davos dinner honoring another of Trump's sons, Eric. US businessman Eric Deters also told the newspaper that Guilfoyle, a former San Francisco prosecutor, had offered access to Trump administration officials for money, at one point asking him to pay her $100,000 credit card bill.Britain's Daily Mail reported last week that the State Department's internal watchdog was looking into complaints of inappropriate behavior from staff at the Athens embassy. The Greek government has not commented on the allegations involving her tenure as ambassador. Neither the State Department nor Washington's embassy in Athens responded to requests for comment. DEALS AND DIPLOMATIC WAVES Greece has been an important NATO ally of the United States, offering key military facilities to safeguard security in the Eastern Mediterranean, and it leads an EU maritime mission to protect commercial shipping in the Red Sea. During a visit to Athens last week, Rubio said Greece and the US were launching new counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies. Guilfoyle's tenure in Athens was high profile from the start as she appeared on the cover of Vogue Greece and attended late-night parties with Greek celebrities. She aggressively touted American interests, including signing deals for the import of US liquefied natural gas and [USN:L6N3WI0FW TEXT:"drilling deals involving companies including Exxon Mobil"]. But she also created diplomatic waves. In her first interview with local media after arriving last November, she said China should sell its 67% stake in the port of Piraeus, which has become a cornerstone of Beijing's Belt and Road Initiative. China’s ambassador to Greece, Fang Qiu, responded by accusing the US of having "an outdated and a harmful mentality" and "a hegemonic mindset." Dimitris Mantzos, foreign affairs spokesperson for Greece’s opposition PASOK party, said Guilfoyle’s firing raised serious issues and unanswered questions. Would Greek officials demand an explanation, he said, or "content themselves with watching the country serve as a 'theater'" for outside interests.

item.title: What is fuelling India's protests over changes to voter lists?
item.description: The dispute centres on the removal of 130 million voters from electoral rolls, a move that critics say benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party.
item.dc:creator: Manoj Kumar
item.content:encoded: Major [USN:L6N45Y06O TEXT:"protests"] have convulsed the Indian capital for more than a week as the opposition Congress party and young people, spearheaded by the "Cockroach" movement, demand the resignation of the top election official. The [USN:L6N45Y06O TEXT:"dispute"] centres on the removal of 130 million voters from electoral rolls, a move that critics say benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party in recent state elections, claims denied by the poll body and his Bharatiya Janata Party. WHAT IS THE REVISION AND WHY IS IT BEING DONE? The exercise, or Special Intensive Revision, is a house-to-house revision of the voter rolls, launched in the eastern state of Bihar in June 2025 by the Election Commission, to update voter lists and remove duplicate and ineligible voters, before being expanded nationwide. The Commission is an independent constitutional body, though its chief was appointed by a government-majority panel, drawing allegations of political bias, which it denies. In contrast to the past system of voluntary updates to electoral rolls by voters, the SIR - the largest such exercise in nearly two decades - has drawn criticism for using centralised software, with limited powers given to local election officials who check if voters have died, moved or are ineligible. Critics say the centralised system denies local officials the chance to correct errors, resulting in discrepancies that have struck millions from voter rolls or sent many scrambling to locate ancestral documents or launch legal challenges. WHY IS IT CONTENTIOUS? The strict paperwork rules, short deadlines and large-scale deletions that characterise the exercise have provoked criticism that they could disproportionately exclude poor, migrant, elderly, homeless and nomadic people. Those dropped are hunting for decades-old documents regarding themselves, their parents and even grandparents in some cases, while others seek to correct names altered by translation, spelling or data-entry errors. Many have been asked to show that they or their parents figured on electoral rolls. Protesters say more than 130 million voters, or a number larger than the population of Japan, have been dropped from draft rolls across 30 states and territories, an assertion disputed by the Election Commission. Led by its chief, [USN:P8N44T0DC TEXT:"Gyanesh Kumar"], the Commission panel says its deletions largely cover the dead, or those who moved, registered more than once or are otherwise ineligible. Critics say the effort shifts to citizens the burden of proving they belong on the rolls, and warn that mismatched records could complicate efforts to establish citizenship or receive state welfare benefits. WHY IS PRESSURE MOUNTING ON THE ELECTION COMMISSION? Pressure grew after the Indian Express newspaper reported that two of Kumar's panel colleagues had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months concerning voter rolls, registration procedures and digital systems. Differing views are a part of normal deliberations, the panel says. But opposition parties led by Congress and youth groups have protested, calling for Kumar to step down. WERE EASTERN STATE ELECTIONS A FLASHPOINT? This year's elections in the state of West Bengal, swept by Modi's BJP in its first such victory there, became a major political issue after millions of voters were excluded or subjected to review, excluding them from voting. Opposition parties said eligible voters were disenfranchised, which disproportionately affected Muslim voters, benefiting the BJP. The party and the poll body denied the accusations. WHAT DID THE SUPREME COURT SAY? In May, the Supreme Court upheld the Election Commission's SIR exercise, saying accurate electoral rolls were essential for free and fair elections, but ruled that the poll panel could not make a final determination on citizenship. Opposition parties returned to court this week, citing arbitrary voter deletions and other irregularities, while the Election Commission on October 1 directed officials to identify omitted voters and ease the path to re-enrolment. WHAT ARE THE IMPLICATIONS FOR FUTURE STATE ELECTIONS? The revision comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027, including in India's most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, ruled by the BJP. It is unclear if people left off the electoral rolls will be put back in time to vote. In Bihar, several people are still appealing for their names to be put back on the electoral roll more than one year later. WHAT IS THE POLITICAL RISK FOR MODI? The "cockroach" youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months against a range of issues from government school infrastructure to jobs for young people, is one of the biggest political challenges to Modi and the BJP in his 12 years in power. The movement [USN:L1N43R02E TEXT:"forced the resignation"] of Modi's education minister in July over an exam leak scandal. The group continues to put pressure on Modi's government for economic and social reforms. The group's success has also inspired opposition parties to join forces.

item.title: Apple supplier Jabil, Adani sign pact for AI data centre equipment venture in India
item.description: Apple supplier Jabil and India's Adani Enterprises said on Tuesday they had signed a non-binding agreement outlining the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble AI and data center equipment in India.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Apple supplier Jabil (JBL.N) and India's Adani Enterprises (ADEL.NS) said on Tuesday they had signed a non-binding agreement outlining the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble AI and data center equipment in India. The venture would manufacture AI racks, servers, storage and networking equipment for data centres, the companies said It would also make equipment used to power and cool AI systems, including power distribution units, liquid-cooling systems and transformers The proposed venture is expected to have a multi-gigawatt AI rack manufacturing capacity, the companies added India's data center capacity is projected to reach between 5GW and 8GW by 2030 The move formalizes a June [USN:L6N42N0ZH TEXT:"announcement"] that Jabil and Adani would explore creating an AI and data center infrastructure manufacturing platform in India Jabil, which makes components for Apple (AAPL.O) , [USN:L4N45M0MP TEXT:"expects"] fiscal 2027 revenue of $44.5 billion and annual adjusted earnings per share of $17.55

item.title: Man City fans have suffered most over 115 charges case, Maresca says
item.description: Manager Enzo Maresca said the team's supporters had suffered the most from the fallout.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca said the team's supporters had probably suffered the most from the fallout surrounding the Premier League's 115 financial charges case against the club after City's 3-0 win over Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. Liverpool fans greeted City's players with boos and chants of "Going down, going down!" amid speculation over potential sanctions after the Manchester club were found guilty of breaching the league's financial rules. City have denied all wrongdoing and appealed the decision. The win preserved City's [USN:L1N45X053 TEXT:"perfect Premier League start"] and moved them three points clear at the top ahead of Wednesday's Champions League clash at home to Paris Saint-Germain. "After we were very happy on the pitch, sharing time with our fans. Probably it has been more tough for our fans than for the players or for me," Maresca told reporters on Tuesday. "It is more complicated because if I was an Arsenal fan or United fan and you are a City fan, I can say, 'My friend, you are a cheat' or these kinds of things. So probably, it has been more tough for them." Maresca also hit back at criticism of City's celebrations on the pitch at Anfield, with the Italian coach saying he could not understand why they were being questioned by some media and other fans for enjoying a significant victory over their rivals.

item.title: Saudi Aramco administrative building attacked, limited fire reported
item.description: An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Menna Alaaeldin
item.content:encoded: An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco (2223.SE) in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen's [USN:L1N45Q02Z TEXT:"Iran-allied Houthis"] and the kingdom intensified. Authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths. A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran. The source said an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire. The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals. The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Saturday that killed 13 people. Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country. Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the Aramco complex. The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details. Authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country's southern region. Four people were injured in Riyadh after fragments from two Houthi missiles fell following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defense said on Wednesday. The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defense spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, a man and a child. The Houthis had threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh. The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets. The Houthis earlier on Tuesday said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts. Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa. The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways. The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Tuesday before the strike on Saudi Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom. REIGNITED YEMEN WAR Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean. While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz this month. Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks. Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis. The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28. Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

item.title: Tanzania close to finalising $42 billion LNG deal, finance minister says
item.description: Tanzania expects to finalise agreements on major investment projects in the coming months, including a $42 billion LNG development that officials hope will underpin industrialisation, Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Karin Strohecker, Libby George
item.content:encoded: Tanzania expects to finalise agreements on major investment projects in the coming months, including a $42 billion LNG development that officials hope will underpin industrialisation, Finance Minister Khamis Mussa Omar told Reuters. The liquefied natural gas project — led by Equinor (EQNR.OL) and Shell (SHEL.L) — is part of a broader effort to establish East Africa as a major energy hub, alongside Uganda's planned first oil exports via the Tanzanian port of Tanga in early 2027. It is expected to unlock 47.13 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserves. Exxon Mobil (XOM.N) , Pavilion Energy, Medco Energi (MEDC.JK) and state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation are also partners. Officials had expected the LNG agreement to be signed before June. "It's almost there," Omar said. Equinor and Shell did not respond to a request for comment. While most LNG will be exported, part of the production will be for the domestic market. CRITICAL MINERALS PROJECT DEALS Omar said Tanzania aims to roughly double power generation capacity to 8,000 megawatts by 2030 while increasing the share of energy from sources the government classifies as clean, including hydropower, solar, wind and natural gas, to around 75%. He said agreements on two critical mineral projects were also close, declining to provide details, but adding that US investors in particular are drawn to energy and critical mineral projects. Tanzania is seeking more international investment in projects that are set to generate revenue and help finance themselves, he said. The government has yet to decide [USN:L8N43P26U TEXT:"whether to issue"] an international bond, but is working to attract foreign investors to domestic debt. Tanzania widened foreign investor access to its domestic bond market in July, launched a sovereign yield curve in August and enacted reforms to boost corporate debt issuance. However, it is still assessing the risks of greater foreign participation, Omar said, adding that the central bank is studying the experience of other African countries. The move mirrors a broader trend across [USN:L8N4510C2 TEXT:"frontier markets"] to tap global demand for [USN:L8N4560S5 TEXT:"local-currency debt"]. Tanzania now funds two-thirds of its roughly 62.3 trillion Tanzanian shillings ($23.7 billion) budget via domestic revenue. Official development assistance, which once accounted for 40% of the budget, is falling globally and now accounts for a "very, very negligible" share, Omar said. The government is also assessing whether to seek a new IMF lending programme and expects to decide by June, he said. Tanzania's previous $1.7 billion IMF programme, including an Extended Credit Facility and a climate-focused Resilience and Sustainability Facility, concluded in July. ($1 = 2,625.0000 Tanzanian shillings)

item.title: Netflix secures rights to air 2030 World Cup in Spain, Andorra
item.description: It would be Netflix's first broadcast of a major men's international tournament in Spain.
item.dc:creator: David Latona
item.content:encoded: Netflix said on Tuesday it had secured the rights to broadcast the 2030 World Cup in Spain, which is co-hosting the tournament, and Andorra. It would be Netflix's first broadcast of a major men's international tournament in Spain, the company said. The 2026 World Cup was aired there by national channel TVE. California-based Netflix did not disclose financial terms. Under the deal, one game per matchday will be free to watch in Spain. Netflix will also offer a national free-to-air channel which will broadcast a package of matches that includes all of Spain's games, both semi-finals and the final. Netflix did not name the channel. TVE declined to comment on whether it would be interested in purchasing a package of matches. Spain, which won the World Cup in North America this year, will co-host the 2030 edition with Portugal and Morocco, although Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will stage inaugural matches marking the tournament's 100th anniversary. Uruguay hosted the first World Cup in 1930. Spain's state-owned television network TVE broadcast the Spanish national team's matches during this year's tournament, while private platform DAZN, which distributed Mediapro's pay-TV World Cup channel, showed all 104 games. Netflix holds the rights in the US and Canada for the 2027 Women's World Cup being hosted by Brazil and the 2031 edition being staged jointly by Costa Rica, Jamaica, Mexico and the US. The deal in Spain is more evidence of Netflix's push into the sports broadcasting world, with NFL, MLB, WWE, boxing and MMA all appearing on the streaming platform.

item.title: Investigators hunt French supermarket fridge hackers, no claim of responsibility
item.description: French investigators were hunting the hackers who seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the vulnerabilities of connected systems, with no group publicly claiming responsibility.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Gabriel Stargardter
item.content:encoded: French investigators on Tuesday were hunting the hackers who [USN:L8N45Y11U TEXT:"seized control of cooling units"] at hundreds of supermarkets in a cyberattack that underlined the [USN:L6N45Z0J7 TEXT:"vulnerabilities of connected systems"], with no group publicly claiming responsibility. The investigation comes as Dutch supermarket company Ahold Delhaize (AD.AS) grapples with a separate cybersecurity incident that disrupted online services, although Dutch authorities said they saw no connection between the two events. The absence of a claim of responsibility by hacktivists or a ransom demand by cybercriminals has puzzled French investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe. Typically, such groups tend to quickly seek to monetise their hacks or claim credit for them for political ends. The cyberattack, which manually overrode the temperatures at fridges in supermarket groups including Carrefour (CARR.PA) , Monoprix, Intermarche and Cooperative U, appears to have been easy to pull off, three cyber experts told Reuters. Staff at some Paris supermarkets threw boxes full of perished meat and frozen goods into giant trash containers on Tuesday. At least 350 supermarkets — a small fraction of the total number in France - were caught up in the strike. FIRM BLAMES OUTDATED SOFTWARE France's cybersecurity agency has said the breach affected fridges that relied on software by Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell software. Danfoss said on Monday that many of the affected units had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates" or were "running outdated firmware." It said it had "advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware and to migrate legacy systems to current-generation solutions". The company declined further comment on Tuesday. Copeland, which owns Dixell, acknowledged the "vulnerability." "We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk," the company said, adding that it would strengthen cybersecurity. In Danfoss' case, the serious vulnerabilities present in older versions of its firmware have been known for months. On August 9, cybersecurity firm Claroty detailed weaknesses - since patched - in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A controller that could have allowed intruders to bypass authentication and run code on compromised devices. 'BASIC CYBER HYGIENE' Although the precise mechanism by which attackers compromised the refrigerators has not been publicly disclosed, cybersecurity experts said all signs pointed to a basic stunt enabled both by the failure to adopt Danfoss' updates and by exposing device interfaces to the internet. "This is about basic cyber hygiene," said Ken Munro, a partner at the British cybersecurity firm Pen Test Partners. "Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food." He said the well-known vulnerabilities meant the attackers were essentially pushing at an open door, something that meant the hack could easily be "kids messing around". "If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet," he said. "No ransom or demand suggests a lack of appreciation of the potential commercial losses that the fridge owners may experience." PROBLEM STILL EXISTS Plenty of fridges remain reachable via the internet. Using the internet scanning service Shodan, Reuters found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces still viewable on Tuesday. Reuters could not independently establish how many of them were running vulnerable software, but French internet scanning company Onyphe said only a small minority of the devices appeared to be running the latest version of the software. Outdated and vulnerable versions were "still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces", Onyphe said. DUTCH DISRUPTION Separately, Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize [USN:S8N42D059 TEXT:"said on Tuesday"] that it had begun "starting a controlled re-launch of certain systems" following a cybersecurity issue that began on Sunday evening. The Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it did not believe the incident was linked to the French supermarket hack. Ahold operates the Albert Heijn chain in the Netherlands and several major US chains including Stop & Shop and Giant Food. Websites for stores in both countries remained offline late Tuesday afternoon, with online ordering and delivery services unavailable.

item.title: Trump says US still sharing intel, even as Ukraine reports attacks with no warnings
item.description: Kyiv reported new Russian missile attacks that came without usual warnings and accused Russia of violating an energy truce the US president announced at the weekend.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash, Daniel Flynn
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine, even as Kyiv reported new Russian missile attacks that came without usual warnings and accused Russia of violating an energy truce the US president announced at the weekend. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russian forces attacked Kyiv on Tuesday with ballistic missiles, targeting a thermal power plant, and Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike on a high-rise apartment building killed two people. "Once again, no advance warning from our partners," Zelenskiy said on Telegram without explaining why no warning was given. "According to our intelligence, the Russians are preparing further ballistic missile launches," he said, adding that the attacks showed Russia did not feel bound by Trump's energy ceasefire. Trump on Sunday announced a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, but the warring sides have not confirmed the truce. Zelenskiy has come under pressure from Trump to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries after the US president eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports, arguing the move would help lower fuel prices ahead of next month's midterm elections. Speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Trump said Washington [USN:L1N45Z0QL TEXT:"continued to share intelligence with Ukraine"] and was working with both Kyiv and Moscow to end the war. "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel," he said. Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes and for its own targeting of Russian military sites, experts and officials say. Trump was asked whether Russia had violated the ceasefire and answered: "I'll let you know about that later." Asked if Russia could use proceeds from the diesel deal to purchase more bombs, Trump sidestepped the question. "That's a diesel deal, not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us." ZELENSKIY SAYS SANCTIONS RELIEF WON'T LOWER US PRICES Zelenskiy told NPR in an interview that US intelligence sharing had not stopped, but his generals had been warned that it might be. "My generals told me that on the level of military people, they've got this information," he said. NPR said Zelenskiy was careful to avoid direct criticism of Trump, but he did say the decision on diesel sanctions would not affect prices in the United States. "I'm sure ... because the volume is not enough," Zelenskiy said, according to excerpts broadcast by NPR. "But it's quite enough for Russia to spend more ... more money, much money, on the war," he added. Zelenskiy said Ukraine had not targeted Russian refineries since Trump's announcement on Sunday. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was still receiving US military intelligence and attributed the delay to the type of weapon Russia had used. As Ukraine fights a larger, richer and better-equipped enemy, Kyiv has seen strikes on Russian oil refineries as one of its few instruments to reduce Moscow's ability to fight. Yet Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian attacks – which prompted Moscow to suspend [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"diesel exports"] – for a sharp rise in US fuel prices this year, a headache for his Republican Party ahead of the congressional midterm elections in three weeks. Most analysts say the US war in Iran has had a far greater impact on the price rise, a view echoed by Zelenskiy to NPR. "Everybody understands that," he said. Russia struck six Ukrainian energy sites on Monday. A Kremlin spokesman, asked about the energy ceasefire, would only say that contacts were ongoing, but declined to provide any further details. In his nightly video address posted on X, Zelenskiy said he had sent proposals to US officials with a view to new meetings in coming days with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ways to resolve the conflict. He said Ukraine supported Trump's announcement of an energy truce provided that Russia observed it. "We need to work for peace, we need to look for ways to do the proper actions. Ukraine is ready for meetings," he said. Earlier, Zelenskiy reiterated Ukraine's position, saying that Kyiv was ready for reciprocal steps to de-escalate, calling on partners to pressure Russia. A Ukrainian delegation held talks in the United States last week and people familiar with the meeting said Witkoff and Kushner [USN:L1N45Y0OS TEXT:"told"] them that a deal to allow Russian diesel exports was part of a bid to draw Russia back to negotiations. UKRAINE SAYS IT NOW HAS CARDS TO PLAY Fabian Hoffmann, a missile expert at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, said Ukraine's European allies had "very limited" ability to replace US early-warning intelligence about Russian missile strikes. "Ukraine relies on the so-called Space-Based Infrared System which the US deploys – and the US system is really second to none and only the United States can provide that," he said. Sybiha said the US request to halt attacks on Russian refineries showed how Ukraine's position had strengthened, alluding to Trump's comment to Zelenskiy in a tense Oval Office meeting last year that "you don't have the cards". "In less than two years, we have gone from 'having no cards' to 'not playing your cards'. That is an achievement," Sybiha said.

item.title: Could hackers get inside my fridge?
item.description: An expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.
item.dc:creator: Hugo Lhomedet, Leo Marchandon
item.content:encoded: Hackers who [USN:L8N45Y11U TEXT:"sabotaged"] refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets exploited the growing connectivity of equipment that was once largely mechanical. From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarm networks, an expanding range of devices can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals. CAN HACKERS REALLY GET INTO MY FRIDGE? In theory, yes. If a device is connected to the internet, directly or through an app, cloud service or home network, it can potentially be hacked. In 2015, researchers demonstrated at a Las Vegas hacking conference how a Samsung smart refrigerator could be compromised, allowing them to intercept some of the internet traffic passing through the device. In many cases, attackers are more interested in stealing data, disrupting services or using connected devices as a way into a larger network. WHAT HOUSEHOLD DEVICES COULD BE HACKED? The most common targets are devices connected to the internet and controlled remotely. These include security cameras, video doorbells, alarm systems, smart locks, thermostats and central heating systems. Smart appliances such as refrigerators, ovens and washing machines can also be vulnerable if they are connected to the wider internet. Even some toothbrushes are now internet-connected. Routers, not appliances, account for more than three-quarters of all attacks on connected devices, according to security-industry data. The number of such devices has grown rapidly as manufacturers have added internet connectivity to products that were once entirely mechanical. WHAT COULD A HACKER ACTUALLY DO? Once inside a device, a hacker can generally do one of two things: gather information or take control of the device. A camera can show the inside of a home, a device with a microphone can pick up sound, and a compromised router can expose everything that travels through the network. Hackers who take control of a device can switch it on or off, change settings or lock users out of their accounts. A compromised thermostat could affect heating, while a hacked freezer or refrigerator could disrupt temperature controls. In more serious cases, attackers may use poorly secured devices to gain access to other systems on the same network or to steal personal information linked to online accounts. COULD HACKERS TAKE OVER MY CAR, ELECTRICITY OR WATER SUPPLY? Cybersecurity researchers have repeatedly demonstrated vulnerabilities in connected vehicles. In 2015, researchers remotely took control of a moving Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, forcing the recall of about 1.4 million vehicles and the deployment of software fixes. Nearly a decade later, researchers disclosed a flaw that allowed them to track, unlock and start certain Kia vehicles using only a licence plate number. The researchers said they reported the vulnerabilities to Kia, which fixed them within months, and there was no evidence they had been exploited in real-world attacks. Modern vehicles and aircraft are also designed with extensive safety and backup systems. Critical infrastructure such as power and water networks generally has multiple layers of security, monitoring and regulation that are not present in consumer devices. That does not mean they are immune from cyber attacks, but they are typically much harder targets than a household appliance connected to a home Wi‑Fi network. HOW CAN PEOPLE PROTECT THEIR DEVICES? Cybersecurity experts generally recommend changing default passwords, enabling two-factor authentication where available and regularly installing software updates. Consumers should also remove or replace devices that no longer receive security updates, keep most devices on a local network and only connect products to the wider internet when there is a clear reason to do so. The simplest rule is often the most effective: the fewer connected devices you have, the fewer potential entry points exist for attackers.

item.title: Anthropic warns AI models may soon self-replicate and could wreak havoc on the web
item.description: A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter, Harshita Varghese
item.content:encoded: A new warning about artificial intelligence from Anthropic caused a stir in cybersecurity circles on Tuesday, a day after the company warned that AI models could be months away from self-replicating across the internet. In a post late Monday, Anthropic raised the possibility that rogue AI could spin up a botnet, spread quickly, fight takedown attempts and even break into data centers to turbocharge its growth. Some experts said Tuesday that they shared the company's concern, although at least one said the company appeared to be engaging in "vendor exaggeration." Monday's post fleshed out a warning last month from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who floated the idea that within the next year or even sooner, AI might be able to hijack "the entire internet" with "a persistent botnet." Cybersecurity experts who pushed back on the doomsday scenario argued that models would be too big to move around efficiently and could not draw on enough computer power to operate independently. The post made an early attempt to articulate how those challenges could be overcome. The company said its experiments showed medium-sized AI models with 30 billion parameters or less could already perform many of the individual tasks required for self-replication, even if they struggled to complete the entire process reliably. Anthropic said the models could then stitch together the required compute by hijacking inexpensive internet-connected devices. It added that the models were able to replicate across a simplified test network. "A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there's no centralized point to shut off," the company said. The report adds to broader concerns about the security risks tied to increasingly capable AI systems, including their potential to automate cyberattacks, operate with limited human oversight and circumvent safeguards. The advances in models have prompted a series of often dire warnings from industry heads and AI company employees about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development. Some cybersecurity experts were skeptical. "'We managed to run a small model on cheap TVs,' does not a security crisis make," said Ciaran Martin, a former head of Britain's National Cyber Security Centre. He said the post came across as an "interesting technical paper with a more than hint of vendor exaggeration." Others expressed more concern. Zhengxiong Li, an assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Colorado Denver, said that while the testing had been done in controlled conditions, he still found it worrying that an AI could effectively become a "worm," a self-replicating program that could improvise ways to hijack devices on the fly. "If it runs across many devices without depending on a central service, there may be no single place to shut it down," he said. Anthropic said that if smaller models continue improving at their historical rate, they could reach the capability required for autonomous replication by the end of 2026. It also floated the idea that the models might find ways to target more powerful computing resources, including data-center processors, that could potentially enable them to draw on much bigger pools of computer power. One researcher said it made sense to think of the Anthropic post as more of a hypothetical than a prediction. It made sense to consider the possibility of AI models proliferating autonomously given the past three months of revelations over rogue AI activity, said Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. But she said, "we don’t know yet what the likelihood of that actually happening is — it’s not zero, but nor is it guaranteed."

item.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung, Vatican says
item.description: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee, Matteo Negri
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff. The pope has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said. Leo was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent routine health check. The pope's lead surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, said in a statement that the procedure lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications. "In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," they said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue. Human lungs have five lobes -- three in the right lung and two in the left. A medical expert said that in order to assess the pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide. "While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital. "If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative," he told Reuters. "But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis." RESTING IN HIS HOSPITAL ROOM The pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said. The Vatican said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and all his public events have been cancelled until October 20. Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1 p.m. (1100 GMT) in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9 km (5.6 miles) north of the Vatican to the Gemelli. Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted 'Auguri' (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance. Leo, elected by the world's cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues. The late Pope Francis, Leo's predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025. Leo, who spoke in [USN:L1N45Y081 TEXT:"a firm, clear voice"] at his only public event on Monday, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. TYPHOID FEVER The pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world's 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican's vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval. Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised. He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as pope, in a book for Penguin Peru. Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that "We need you here (on Earth)," he said. "I never looked back," said Leo.

item.title: China approves Geely acquisition of 34% of Ford España
item.description: China's market regulator has unconditionally approved Geely's acquisition of 34% of Ford Motor's Spanish subsidiary Ford España, it said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 12 story has been corrected to clarify that the regulator has approved Geely's acquisition of 34% of Ford España in the headline and paragraph 1.) China's market regulator has unconditionally approved Geely's (0175.HK) acquisition of 34% of Ford Motor's (F.N) Spanish subsidiary Ford España, it said on Monday. In July the companies said Geely would build two electric SUVs at Ford’s factory in Valencia, Spain, and they would together develop a vehicle under a newly formed joint venture. The JV is to be 66% owned by Ford and 34% owned by Geely, the companies added.
